name: Voltage
question: How much electrical tension? Each gridline step is ten times more.

items.name: Brain waves (EEG) at the scalp
items.fact: Brain waves are measured in millionths of a volt.

items.name: Nerve cell at rest
items.fact: Every nerve cell is a tiny battery, kept charged by pumping ions.

items.name: Lemon battery
items.fact: A lemon with a copper and a zinc electrode makes almost a volt.

items.name: AA battery
items.fact: AAA, AA, C and D alkaline batteries all give the same 1.5 V; bigger ones just last longer.

items.name: USB phone charger
items.fact: USB has carried 5 volts since the first version in 1996.

items.name: Car battery
items.fact: A car battery has six cells of about 2 volts each.

items.name: European wall socket
items.fact: North America uses about 120 V; most of the rest of the world uses 220–240 V.

items.name: Electric eel attack
items.fact: Electric eels aren't true eels; they're a kind of knifefish.

items.name: London Underground track
items.fact: Many Tube lines use two live rails, one positive and one negative.

items.name: Electric fence
items.fact: Electric fences use high voltage but very short, low-current pulses.

items.name: High-speed train overhead line
items.fact: Most European high-speed lines run at 25,000 volts AC.

items.name: Long-distance power line
items.fact: Very high voltages cut the energy lost when power travels far.

items.name: Biggest human-made DC voltage
items.fact: It was produced by a Van de Graaff generator at Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

items.name: Lightning bolt
items.fact: A typical lightning bolt spans about 100 million volts end to end.
